summary: This best current practice pins down what the acronym OAM means in IETF documents: Operations, Administration, and Maintenance. People had used it loosely and inconsistently, so the document defines the term and its component parts for use in all future IETF work.

plainLanguage.summary: OAM has been expanded in different ways across networking documents. This Best Current Practice recommends that IETF documents use it to mean Operations, Administration, and Maintenance.

subtitle: The IETF's recommended meaning and use of the acronym OAM.

tldr.problem: Networking documents use OAM with different expansions. That inconsistency can leave readers uncertain about which functions a specification includes.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC reviews uses of the term and recommends a consistent expansion for IETF documents. It also distinguishes O&M and Mgmt and describes what Operations, Administration, and Maintenance cover.
tldr.outcome: IETF documents are to use OAM for Operations, Administration, and Maintenance. RFC 6291 is a Best Current Practice updated by RFC 10014.

today: RFC 6291 is Best Current Practice 161, updated by RFC 10014. It recommends that future IETF documents use OAM to mean Operations, Administration, and Maintenance.

sections.title: Why OAM Needs a Consistent Definition
sections.content:
OAM is widely used in data and telecommunications, but its meaning has not always been consistent. Different interpretations of a key term can cause confusion when documents describe network functions.

RFC 6291 recommends one expansion for future IETF documents and explains how the three parts relate to network operations. It also gives preferred forms for related abbreviations.
sections.plainLanguage: Readers need to know which functions a document includes when it says OAM. This RFC recommends one meaning for IETF documents.

sections.title: How Other Standards Bodies Used OAM
sections.content:
Other standards development organizations used OAM before the IETF guidance. Some expanded it as Operations and Maintenance, while others used Operations, Administration, and Maintenance or described it as tools for installing, monitoring, and troubleshooting a network.

These uses cover related network-management work but do not use the same words for the acronym. The RFC reviews them to explain the source of inconsistent usage.
sections.plainLanguage: Other standards groups used OAM with different expansions. The RFC records those differences before setting a preferred IETF meaning.

sections.title: What Operations, Administration, and Maintenance Cover
sections.content:
Operations keeps the network and its services running, including monitoring and finding problems. Administration tracks network resources and how they are used. Maintenance supports repairs and upgrades, such as replacing equipment or changing a device configuration.

The RFC notes that the scope of Operations can vary and that the letters describe connected functions. Maintenance aims to reduce failures and their effects and to support the right response when failures occur.
sections.plainLanguage: Operations keeps services running, Administration tracks resources, and Maintenance supports repairs and upgrades. These functions work together but describe different responsibilities.

sections.title: Different Expansions in IETF Documents
sections.content:
Earlier IETF RFCs expanded OAM in several ways. The examples include Operations, Administration, and Maintenance; Operations and Maintenance; and Operations and Management. One document also used OAM&P to include Provisioning.

The list in RFC 6291 is explicitly not exhaustive. These examples show why a shared recommendation was useful.
sections.plainLanguage: Earlier IETF documents did not always use the same expansion of OAM. This RFC gives examples of that variation to explain the need for consistent usage.

sections.title: Recommended Terms
sections.content:
The RFC recommends OAM for Operations, Administration, and Maintenance. It recommends O&M when referring to OAM and Management together, and Mgmt when an abbreviation for Management is needed.

Provisioning means configuring network resources to support offered services. It is outside the scope of OAM in this document; in general, provisioning prepares new services while OAM keeps the network able to support existing services.
sections.plainLanguage: Use OAM for Operations, Administration, and Maintenance. Use O&M for OAM and Management together, and describe Provisioning separately.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
This terminology guidance has no direct security implications. The RFC notes that misunderstanding OAM could lead to an incorrect specification or implementation, which could create security problems in protocols or networks.

A consistent meaning can therefore help make future specifications clearer, even though the document does not define a security mechanism.
sections.plainLanguage: This document does not add a security feature. Clear terminology can reduce the chance that an implementation misunderstands what a specification requires.
